name: 1770 Extreme Aurora

phenomena.details: Estimated Dst far below -500 nT based on aurora visibility at ~24° magnetic latitude.
Inferred large X-class flare; no photometric record.

impacts.description: Red aurora visible from Japan (Kyoto, ~24° magnetic latitude) for nine consecutive nights; described in dozens of samurai diaries and official records as a 'red flames across the sky'.
Widely recorded in Japanese historical documents including domain records and personal diaries; provided critical calibration for historical geomagnetic storm intensity estimates.

papers.title: The extreme space weather event in September 1770
papers.authors: Hayakawa, H., Ebihara, Y., Willis, D. M., et al.
papers.keyFinding: Compiled Japanese historical records of aurora visible for 9 nights at latitudes as low as ~24° magnetic latitude, suggesting a storm rivaling or exceeding the Carrington Event.

summary: A geomagnetic storm in September 1770 produced aurora visible across Japan for nine consecutive nights, with observations at magnetic latitudes as low as ~24°, suggesting an intensity potentially comparable to the 1859 Carrington Event.
description: Contemporary Japanese records – including samurai diaries, domain reports, and astronomical logs – describe vivid red aurora that persisted for nine nights starting on September 17, 1770, visible from locations corresponding to magnetic latitudes of ~24°. Modern analysis by Hayakawa et al. (2017) compiled over 50 historical sources and estimated a peak Dst of roughly −440 to −600 nT or lower, making this storm one of the most intense pre-instrumental events on record. The event occurred near the maximum of Solar Cycle 1 (the first cycle in the modern numbering convention). The nine-day duration of visible aurora indicates sustained severe to extreme geomagnetic disturbance, potentially from multiple CME arrivals.
